298:## 6. For Pavol
22:- The restart is `Documentation/Specification/`, begun 2012-02-20 by Luchangco, abandoned 2012-05-31 with most chapters empty. Its Types chapter (`Prose/Language/types.tick`, 1,056 lines) is fresh 2012 prose and the team's last word on types, exclusion and `comprises`. It has no chapter on static parameters, numbers, coercion beyond a relation, or the library.
24:- So "the designers' latest word" is not one text. On types and the exclusion rule it is the 2012 Types chapter and Naden. On the library, static parameters, coercion, overloading resolution and the number chapters it is the Working Draft, whose text on those topics is 2008-2010. On what they actually made run, it is the code: the interpreter's library (2007-2012, never type-checked) and the compiler's prelude and checker (2009-2012).
30:- The compiler side went flat in 2009, after a tower that stood from March to August. Chase, 2009-08-31: "ZZ32 is NOT a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get coercion working" (`6896886fb`). Maessen, 2009-11-17: "expect more coercions to come on line as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric hierarchy" (`128f313b5`). Steele added the prelude's `Comparison` traits with their `extends` clauses commented out on 2011-07-15 (`b3c2e1342`) and added the operators of the sibling `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` on 2011-07-22 (`da5291587`). Steele's 2016 slide draws `Number → {Integral → ZZ32, ZZ64, ZZ; Float → RR32, RR64}` (`SteeleJuliaCon2016-extract.md:159-161`).
41:- **`where` clauses**, a second way to bind a type variable ("Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of themselves", `basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-352`, and `object Empty extends List[\T\] where {T extends Object}`, `:384-397`): "Widening and where clauses are not yet supported" (`basic/conversions-coercions.tex:15`); code generation refuses any declaration with one (FACTS:158).
48:### Coercion
50:- A **coercion** is a conversion a trait declares from another type (`trait ZZ64 ... coerce(z: ZZ32)`), inserted by the compiler where no declaration applies without it. It is not chained (`conversions-coercions.tex:127-130`). "For a given functional call, we first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion. If so, the most specific declaration is selected; if not, then coercions are explicitly added" (`:454-462`). It is resolved on static types: "Notice that coercion is resolved statically", with an example where `c: C = D` and `f(c)` calls `f(A)` by coercion "despite the fact that the declaration f(B) is applicable to the dynamic call f(D)" (`:598-635`). The draft's own example of widths declares `ZZ64 coerce(z: ZZ32)` and `ZZ128` from both (`:549-565`); no sentence makes `ZZ32` a subtype of `ZZ64`. "Fortress supports the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values" (`:64-66`), a general sentence.
51:- Numerals: "numerals have their own types ... This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148`); the types named (`NaturalNumeral[\n,10,v\]`) carry the value and were never implemented; a note says "We need to describe the Numeral type hierarchy" (`:83-95`). The prelude has one `IntLiteral`, a sibling each number type coerces from (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390-429`; Maessen 2009: "ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec"). The interpreter's is `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }` with its arithmetic commented out: "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." (`FortressBuiltin.fss:497-498`).
52:- The prelude's coercions are every exact integer pair and none from an integer into a float (`reviews/flattening-questions-ways.md` § 5, checked at `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108`, `:147-149`, `:433-435`).
118:### D4. Route A: keep the rule, flatten the tower, teach walk coercion (2026-09-24)
125:  - On Naden's unsolved aim: route A does not solve it; it gives it up, keeping the rule and letting ℤ reach ℚ and ℝ64 by coercion. That is what Naden's own self-type-bound rewrite points to ("a flat tower's idiom", the brief § 4), and what his principle of 2026-09-29 accepts: an unfinished corner accepted to get to one program.
127:- What it has cost: `Number` lost its catch-alls, so `Number`'s `=` is not transitive (row 434); 89 team test lines respelled; 21 of the team's 24 demos with an unwritten clause-form sum fail and are not gated (`reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:75`); an integer scalar meeting a float array was refused under walk until batch N; and the interpreter chooses coercions on run-time values (D4's second half, judged under tension 5 below). Reversal to C: FACTS:48's price plus everything built on the flat tower since batch 6.
166:- Verdict: a call, in the team's own layered form; the requirement behind it ("no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation ... preserve the original ... preserve the option to go the route C") is the right one. Three record slips: Appendix I's introduction says every change follows route A, which answers 9 and 10 do not (item 23, a default is filed); the inference chapter's entry claims to state "the rule that the checker builds, and no more" while four gated rows depart from it (`reviews/batch-N-review.md:8`); and the coercion chapter's "resolved statically" passage has no callout where walk contradicts its own example (tension 5).
180:### D16. Answer 8: mixed widths by coercion, with promotion (2026-09-26)
182:- Verdict: coercion is the designers' mechanism (faithful); narrowing the draft's general "integer values to floating-point values" to the exact pairs is a departure by his precision principle, between the draft (all) and the prelude (none), justified and recorded (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:74-90`); promotion (the narrowest type both sides coerce into) fills a gap the specification never wrote, with Julia's rule. One inconsistency inside it: `NN32` into `RR64` is exact and stays explicit, only because the decision named `ZZ32` and the numerals (the callout says so). Tidy it (section 6, item 9).
203:- Verdict: faithful to the specification's direction ("numerals have their own types", coercions defined by the library) in the implementers' shape (one sibling type, not the value-carrying types the draft named and never described). Right, on two conditions the record carries only in part: rung Q's brief must quote the team's warning whole, including its consequence ("all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals"), and measure it; and `exactValue` must answer a numeral before `Number`'s `=` meets one (the conversion judgement's requirement). Under the prelude, literal arithmetic is folded at compile time (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`); walk folds nothing, so the measurement is the interpreter's.
224:- Decision 1: faithful to the coercion chapter's order ("first determine whether there exists a declaration that is applicable without coercion", `:454-462`); the tie rule and promotion fill gaps. His own idea (way 4, C#'s rule) was weighed and not taken, for reasons the designers' text supports. Right, and rightly asked for a soundness check first.
225:- Its landed form departs from it: the checker tries a call by subtyping under the expected type first, so a declaration reached only by coercion whose result fits can win over a generic that fits the arguments as they are (row 508, `XXXInferContextKeepsFit`; item 34). That is a defect against his decision and against the specification's Σ, on the compiled path, gated as an expected failure. Its fix is named. Section 6, item 4.
252:3. **Row 508 (D25's landed form), item 34.** The checker's attempt order contradicts his decision 1 and the coercion chapter. On the path: it is the checker microGPT will run under. Gated; fix named; belongs to phase 3.
263:5. **Walk's coercion choice against his rule of 2026-09-24.** The interpreter contradicts the coercion chapter's own printed example (3 against 4) and the passage carries no callout; item 16 ("route A's price is wider") is parked with a default and no answer. Can wait in substance, since the compiled path follows the text and microGPT's static types are concrete; the callout is one paragraph in batch 7b's rung S.
294:- Has he gone astray? No. On the calls that shape the language, he has gone where the type group's own implementers went and where their last texts point: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat with coercion between widths, sizes in the types, the 2009 overload ban dropped, `comprises` read on values, conversions never changing which declaration runs. Each of these finishes something the team started and left open, and each is recorded with its original and its road back.
308:  2. Keep the decision as it stands, all ℤ, with the reason restated on coercion: every float program that floors and continues in float arithmetic writes `asFloat`. Touches the same lines plus every such caller. Costs the same rung and a notation tax on users.
332:- Rung I tries subtyping under the expected type first, so a declaration reached only by coercion whose result fits can win over a generic that fits the arguments as they are. That contradicts your decision 1 of 2026-09-28 and the coercion chapter's Σ. It is gated as an expected failure.

354:### 7. Is the interpreter's run-time choice of coercions accepted as the interpreter's limit? (item 16; tension 5; batch 7b's rung S)
356:- Walk has no static types, so it cannot resolve a coercion on a static type; it chooses on the value, and contradicts the coercion chapter's own printed example (3 against 4, `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`) and the narrow case rung C found (`XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`). The compiled path follows the text. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so the paths agree on it. The inference chapter carries a callout for the generic half; the coercion chapter's "resolved statically" passage carries none.

364:- The one library's `IntLiteral` carries "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." 6. **Record slips**, none touching a running program: the route-A brief's missing citation of "mutually exclusive"; POSITIONS:47 still giving row 330's fallen reason; Appendix I's introduction (item 23); the inference entry's over-claim; the goal's "July 2012".

### Omission

1. **Phase 4, the switch-over, is the largest piece and is not designed.** Its code-generation half is sized: on the flat tree code generation emits 326 of the library's declarations and refuses 225, of which only 4 are on declarations the checker passed, and the dispatch generator refuses 12 of 198 overload sets, down from 131 of 283 on the nested tower (`perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat.md:12-13`); so the checker's zero carries most of that half with it. Its other half is not sized: two native mechanisms (walk's 108 and 231 bindings against the compiler's helpers; `import java` unfinished under walk, FACTS:157), the four well-known types, the 38 sources that name the prelude, and "at least two batches" as the only size on record. On the path. Not an error of decision; the natives' shape probe the library-route judgement asked for (its step 2(c), a two-declaration component bound with `import java`, run by the interpreter) has not been run, and no brief exists.
2. **Phase 5's collision.** "No model line changes" has been kept in every batch. Decision D will not keep it: 21 lines out, 29 in, by the record's own measurement, stale since `tabulate`. Beside it: arithmetic in a size (item 15, the library's own rank-2 and rank-3 storage; no batch), a size known only at run time opened by the checker (`reflect`, the "two bridges"; `NatReflect`'s "we ought to build it in"), and the element width (`RR32` or `RR64`) he asked about and was not answered. On the path. All are his decisions, and none has a line before "after the switch-over".
3. **Decision A, the mechanism under `double[]`.** The array review found that the library's own device (a `typecase` in a generic factory) cannot return a monomorphic store through the checker, and that the team's direction is a loader template per instantiation (`Unbox.java`, the expando stub). No design, no probe since. On the path, and it is the "fast" half of the goal.
4. **The algebraic layer.** His own aim of 2026-09-15 ("extend the algebraic layer, Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need") has no plan line; route A left `Number` without algebra, and `Vector` and `Matrix` keep `T extends Number` with "no evidence for their arithmetic" (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1547`, `:1665`; `reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:90`). On the path at phase 5: the array design must choose the bounds. The library's own traits exist for it (`AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`); the specified fields and groups do not.
5. **Walk's coercion choice against his rule of 2026-09-24.** The interpreter contradicts the coercion chapter's own printed example (3 against 4) and the passage carries no callout; item 16 ("route A's price is wider") is parked with a default and no answer. Can wait in substance, since the compiled path follows the text and microGPT's static types are concrete; the callout is one paragraph in batch 7b's rung S.
6. **The team's demos.** 21 of 24 with an unwritten clause-form sum fail since the flat tower; no gate stage runs demos (`build.xml` has none). Can wait for microGPT; against his own "one tree with everything running" (2026-09-17).
7. **Off the path, note only**: the saturating operators (specified beside the wrapping ones, no line); code generation refusing any `where` clause (no ledger row); the checker on interpreter programs (his 2026-09-15 wish; it arrives with the switch-over); `where` clauses, covariance, contracts, properties, units, `widens`, `HasIdentity`, `bool` parameters, complex numbers, tensors, distribution. Each is an intention of the designers no plan carries; none is needed to compile microGPT; the ledger's worklist holds most of them.
8. **Row 487.** Closed families are not closed across components; the batch-7b proof names it as its open assumption. Batch 8's, and it should stay there.

## 4. The tensions

Fourteen are on the evidence map's list (b). Grouped by what they need.

Need a decision from him, in this order:

- Tension 2, row 330's reason. Now, before batch 7b, since it is one entry (section 6, item 1).
- Tension 7, answer 12's premise against row 447. Before phase 4 (item 2).
- Tension 4, the implicit bound. Before batch 7b's rung S writes the sentence (item 3).
- Tension 6, decision 1 against row 508. Phase 3, batch 8 at the latest (item 4).
- Tension 11, the algebraic layer against route A's `Number`. With phase 5's array design (item 6).
- Tension 12, the `IntLiteral` warning. Not a decision; a line in rung Q's brief (item 8 carries it).

Fine as they stand, with one line each:

- Tension 1 (one library and F2 against route A's shapes): settled by his yes of 2026-09-24; F2 is about patterns, not about keeping every 2008 shape.
- Tension 3 (answer 8 against the draft's general sentence): recorded in the text; tidy `NN32`.
- Tension 5 (no open discrepancy against walk's run-time choice): fine in substance; one callout and item 16's one-line answer close it (item 7).
- Tension 8 (a size as ℕ32 against a size used as a value as ℤ32): consistent, as he was told; the JVM's indices are `int`.
- Tension 9 (the notation rule against the reversible stops): no model line has landed that way; decision D will be a diff, as his rule requires.
- Tension 10 (answer 6's "resurrect" against no phase for covariance): future work is the right home; the ledger holds it.
- Tension 13 (ranges over `ZZ32` against the factorial's notation): a specification example, not a model line; leave it, or restore the product over a converted range when someone touches the chapter.
- Tension 14 (test first against the landing rules): the tests are still owed and tracked; a process choice he made with the costs in front of him.

## 5. His question, answered

- Has he gone astray? No. On the calls that shape the language, he has gone where the type group's own implementers went and where their last texts point: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat with coercion between widths, sizes in the types, the 2009 overload ban dropped, `comprises` read on values, conversions never changing which declaration runs. Each of these finishes something the team started and left open, and each is recorded with its original and its road back.
- Where? Two places, both small. Row 330 departs from the team's consistent declaration for floats on a reason he no longer has, and it is not built. The written bound of batch 7 hid a real hole behind a lower checker count, and the switch-over will find it. One specification sentence (the implicit bound) was changed by a default rather than by him.
- How far? Not far, and not in the direction of a redesign. The errors are in the record and in one landed rung, not in the language. The risk that remains is of omission: the three least designed pieces, the switch-over, the sized model and the unboxed store, are the ones the goal depends on, and every batch since 2026-09-26 has been spent before them.

## 6. For Pavol

In the order needed. Each is one question, its context, numbered options with what each touches and costs, and a recommendation last.
  1. Run the array design's clean list now (protocol § 6, the library's way first, the nine steps), read-only, with decision D's diff re-based and re-measured on today's tree, so that the decisions reach you while phase 3 runs. Touches nothing on `main` but reviews. Costs two or three worker sessions, about 1M tokens.
  2. After the switch-over, as the plan has it. Costs a serial wait at the point the goal depends on most.
- Recommendation: 1; the diff of the model lines comes to you as your rule requires, and you decide D, A and the width one per message.

### 7. Is the interpreter's run-time choice of coercions accepted as the interpreter's limit? (item 16; tension 5; batch 7b's rung S)

- Walk has no static types, so it cannot resolve a coercion on a static type; it chooses on the value, and contradicts the coercion chapter's own printed example (3 against 4, `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`) and the narrow case rung C found (`XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`). The compiled path follows the text. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so the paths agree on it. The inference chapter carries a callout for the generic half; the coercion chapter's "resolved statically" passage carries none.
- Options:
  1. Accept it: one callout at `conversions-coercions.tex:598-635` in the S1 form, item 16 closed with the two tests as its record. Touches one paragraph in batch 7b's rung S. Costs nothing.
  2. Make walk match: needs static types under walk, which is the checker on interpreter programs, after the switch-over.
- Recommendation: 1 now; 2 is the later road and is already your wish of 2026-09-15.

### 8. Does rung Q's brief carry the team's warning whole, and measure it? (batch N's second run)

- The one library's `IntLiteral` carries "Do not enable these until coercion is implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals." Coercion is implemented; rung Q gives `IntLiteral` its own arithmetic, as the prelude has; the prelude folds literal arithmetic at compile time and walk folds nothing.
127:- What it has cost: `Number` lost its catch-alls, so `Number`'s `=` is not transitive (row 434); 89 team test lines respelled; 21 of the team's 24 demos with an unwritten clause-form sum fail and are not gated (`reviews/batch-6-conformance.md:75`); an integer scalar meeting a float array was refused under walk until batch N; and the interpreter chooses coercions on run-time values (D4's second half, judged under tension 5 below). Reversal to C: FACTS:48's price plus everything built on the flat tower since batch 6.
166:- Verdict: a call, in the team's own layered form; the requirement behind it ("no open discrepancy between the spec and our implementation ... preserve the original ... preserve the option to go the route C") is the right one. Three record slips: Appendix I's introduction says every change follows route A, which answers 9 and 10 do not (item 23, a default is filed); the inference chapter's entry claims to state "the rule that the checker builds, and no more" while four gated rows depart from it (`reviews/batch-N-review.md:8`); and the coercion chapter's "resolved statically" passage has no callout where walk contradicts its own example (tension 5).
285:- Tension 5 (no open discrepancy against walk's run-time choice): fine in substance; one callout and item 16's one-line answer close it (item 7).

content.content:
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.
=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

By the definition above, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} is then not more specific than
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}, and neither the two declarations of \VAR{f} nor the two
coercions to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128} are a valid overloading; both implementations
of the revival refuse the example as the Working Draft wrote it.
The clauses added are spelled as \library\ spell those of their integer types,
each trait excluding the wider ones.}

Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
into the call.
This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
The coercions that the instance of a declaration with static parameters needs
are chosen and inserted into the call in the same way
(\secref{static-arg-inference}).
\revision{revival-overloading}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say
how the coercions of an instance of a declaration with static parameters are
chosen.}

For example, in the following program:
%trait A
%  coerce(c:C) = ...
%end
%trait B excludes A end
%trait C end
%object D extends {B,C} end
%
%f(a:A) = 3
%f(b:B) = 4
%
%c : C = D
%f(c)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
\(f(c)\)
\end{Fortress}
the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
\EXP{f(B)} is
%dynamically directly
applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
coercion.
\revision{revival-coercion-walk}{The compiled path of the revival resolves the
example as this section says and runs \EXP{f(A)}.
The interpreter has no static types, so it chooses a coercion on the value:
for \EXP{f(c)} it finds \EXP{f(B)} applicable to the value without coercion and
runs it, and it answers the same way wherever an argument's static type needs a
coercion and the argument's value is of a type that another declaration already
fits.
The two cases are gated as expected failures of the interpreter
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss} and
\nolinkurl{XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss}, row~19 of the revival's gap
ledger).
The interpreter is to follow this section once the compiled type checker checks
the programs it runs and it takes the coercions that the checker inserts.}




\section{Restrictions on Coercion Declarations}
\seclabel{restrictions-coercion}
We place two restrictions on coercion declarations to ensure that it is
always possible to resolve coercions.

It is a static error for a type to define a coercion from any of its
subtypes.  For example, the following program is statically rejected:
%trait Number
====
component XXXCoercionStaticRungC
export Executable

(*) explorations/compile-ladder/rung-interp-coercion/REPORT.md

trait A
  coerce(c: C) = AOf
end
trait B excludes A end
trait C end
object AOf extends A end
object D extends { B, C } end

f(a: A): ZZ32 = 3
f(b: B): ZZ32 = 4

run() = do
    println("REACHED")
    c: C = D
    assert(f(c), 3, "row 19: coercion is resolved statically, so f(c) with c: C calls f(A) though f(B) applies to D without coercion; conversions-coercions.tex, section \"Coercion Resolution\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
====
component XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC
export Executable

(*) explorations/compile-ladder/rung-interp-coercion/REPORT.md

trait Wide excludes { Narrow }
  coerce(x: Narrow) = WideOf(x.small)
  getter big(): ZZ32
end
trait Narrow excludes { Wide }
  getter small(): ZZ32
end
object WideOf(b: ZZ32) extends Wide
  getter big(): ZZ32 = b
end
object NarrowOf(s: ZZ32) extends Narrow
  getter small(): ZZ32 = s
end

g(x: Wide): String = "g(Wide)"
g(x: NarrowOf): String = "g(NarrowOf)"

run() = do
    println("REACHED")
    n: Narrow = NarrowOf(1)
    assert(g(n), "g(Wide)", "row 19: coercion is resolved on the static type Narrow, so g(n) calls g(Wide) though g(NarrowOf) applies to the value without coercion; conversions-coercions.tex, section \"Coercion Resolution\"")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

Here is the context from the start.

**Who and what.** Kento Emoto wrote `Library/Generator2.fss`, a library for generators of generators. The file says it's copyright 2010, free software, by him. Its test is `ProjectFortress/tests/Generator2Test.fss`. Emoto's file is the library's own fast path for combining generators, and the question is about one piece of it.

**What "distribute" means.** A reduction combines the values of a generator, such as `SUM` or `MAX`. Some pairs of reductions can be fused: the maximum of sums can be computed as a sum of maxima, `max(a+b, a+c) = a + max(b, c)`, so no intermediate sums are built. The library asks each pair whether it can fuse, through a method called `distribute`. `SumReduction` answers that for `MAX` and `MIN` and gives back the fused pair.

**The team's text.** In `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, the team left a generic `distribute` commented out, around line 3235. It sits beside a catch-all `distribute(r: Any)` that says "no fused pair" to everything. The catch-all is a hack the team wrote to avoid an overloading error.

**Library or interpreter?** Both, and the two paths differ. The change edits the library, so it reaches the interpreter, walk, and the compiler. The probe also changed the compiler's checker so it accepts the new `where` conditions, so that part is a compiler change. The distance of 49 to 42 counts the checker's errors on the library. The walk loss is in the interpreter.

**Why something stops.** The catch-all answered every reduction, including the nested ones. A sum of sums over a generator of generators, with no fused pair, fell through to the plain computation. Once the catch-all is gone, walk must pick a generic `distribute` for that nested case. Walk doesn't infer a generic method's own static arguments yet (ledger row 21), so the program stops with an error. The suites don't reach this case, and microGPT's quick pair still passes 7 of 7.

**What should an integer raised to a negative power give, such as `2^(-1)`?**

**Context**
- **This replaces Haiku's ask on this item from today,** whose figures were stale and two of its claims wrong.
- **Where the integer power stands today.** Every integer `^` in the interpreter's library is declared `RR64`, a float. Walk gives `2^3` = `8` and `2^(-1)` = `0.5`. The compiled path gives `2^(-1)` = `0`, because its native converts the result of Java's `Math.pow` to an `int`.
- **The premise you've already taken:** each integer `^` answers its own type, so `2^3` is `8 : ZZ32`.
  - That keeps integer code exact, such as the library's `strToInt`, which sums `d radix^(n-i)`.
  - The exponent stays signed, since it's often computed, as `n-i` is there.
  - So `2^(-1)` needs a `ZZ32` value, or none. That's the fork.
- **The team's earlier text.** The Working Draft of 2011 gave `2^(-1)` = 1/2: ℤ was then inside ℚ, and a signed exponent went to the rationals' power.
- **The team's later word.** The compiled library gives every exponent an integer type. The later word wins, and that's your premise.
  - On the value it says nothing you can weigh. Its 0 is a side effect of the conversion.
  - Guy Steele's helper that answers 0 is unfinished, nothing calls it, and it also gives 0 for `0^(-1)`.
  - The revival's chapter leaves the value open.
- **The library's own way.** A result that a fixed-width integer type can't hold raises `IntegerOverflow`. A fraction comes from a float or rational base: `10.0^(-4)`, or `(2/3)^(-1)` = `3/2`. microGPT writes `10.0^(-5)`.
- **How to judge.** The team's later word comes first, then its library, then the peer languages where the team conflicts or is silent. On the value the team is silent, so the peers weigh.
- **The peers.** Julia, Java's `BigInteger.pow` and Haskell's `^` raise an error. Rust types the exponent unsigned. X10 answers a float, as walk does today. Swift has no integer power. None answers 0.
- **The switch-over needs this answer,** before it and no sooner. Six of today's 34 distance sites are the power's.
  - The distance counts every error the compiled checker finds in the interpreter's library, and it must reach 0 before the switch-over.
  - The checker count is 30 today, all in the component that holds the six sites. The probe didn't measure it. It may fall with the six sites, or rise as the check reaches further.
